item: Rule 62 vetting, shared rows (queued at the CA retro sync, 2026-10-03; answer each, shared text not edited): (1) `surrender-end-of-term` (CA's proposal, 2026-10-03): qualify 'Tenant will surrender possession of the property and return all keys to Landlord immediately' with 'unless applicable law entitles Tenant to remain', because a just-cause or similar statute may let a tenant stay past the term. Is the qualified wording lawful and accurate in your state, and does the current wording state a duty your law doesn't back? (2) `default-by-tenant` (MN's proposal, 2026-10-02; ND and CA support): move the no-cure carve-out ('except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure') out of the non-rent limb into its own sentence reaching both limbs. Is that lawful and accurate in your state (it is self-limiting, so check only that it can't be read to drop a cure or pre-suit notice your law requires for nonpayment)? Already settled, so don't ask Taylor again: if the edit would only drop the lease's own promise of written notice of a rent default that your law doesn't require, Taylor decided for Indiana (2026-10-03) and Pennsylvania (2026-10-04) that the lease follows the statute, with no optional notice clause. Support the edit, and say in your section which education row should tell landlords they may still give notice first (Claude Code updates it at the merge).

Rule 62 vetting, shared row (queued 2026-10-03; New York tagged `default-by-tenant` at its sync): (1) CO's proposal to delete 'and reasonable costs and expenses' from the landlord-remedies sentence: N.Y. Real Prop. Law § 234-a bars legal or administrative fees without a court order and § 234 makes fee clauses reciprocal, so does the phrase risk reading as a barred fee, and does deleting it give anything up? (2) MN's proposal to move the no-cure carve-out into its own sentence reaching both limbs: lawful and accurate in New York, given the 14-day rent demand (N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 711(2)) and the Good Cause Eviction Law? Answer each; shared text not edited.
